info.title: Kibi Connect - API Docs
info.description:
RESTful API for Kibi Connect. Enables external applications and services to interact with your workspace data using bearer token authentication.

## Syncing with an external system — quick reference

If the master data lives outside Kibi — files in OneDrive or SharePoint, Markdown in a Git repository, issues in a forge — you do not have to keep a table of Kibi ULIDs on your side. Wiki pages, tasks, posts, calendar events and groups can each carry an **external id** per integration, and you address them by that id — both when writing and when reading back.

This section is the summary. The full walkthrough — minting the token, the first import, both sync directions, deletes, loop protection and the list of things that catch people out — follows further down under *Syncing an external system with Kibi*, together with the content-format reference.

### The slug, in short

The namespace comes from the **API token**, never from the payload. It is chosen when the token is minted, under **My profile > Integrations**, it can only be set by a **system administrator**, and it **cannot be changed afterwards** — a different slug means a different token. Format: `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, up to 64 characters.

A token without a slug gets **422** from every endpoint below, and reads `external_ref: null` everywhere rather than another integration's mapping.

Holding the slug is a permission, not a label: a token carrying it may work on every mapping of that integration in the tenant. That is why the field is restricted to system administrators.

### Endpoints

| Resource | Write through | Read back by your id | Delete |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wiki page | `PUT /api/v1/wiki/by-external-id` | `GET /api/v1/wiki?external_id=…` | `DELETE /api/v1/wiki/{ulid}` → 204 |
| Task | `PUT /api/v1/tasks/by-external-id` | `GET /api/v1/tasks?external_id=…` | `DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{ulid}` → 204 |
| Post | `PUT /api/v1/posts/by-external-id` | `GET /api/v1/posts?external_id=…` | `DELETE /api/v1/posts/{ulid}` → **200 with body** |
| Calendar event | `PUT /api/v1/calendar/events/by-external-id` | `GET /api/v1/calendar/events?external_id=…` | `DELETE /api/v1/calendar/events/{ulid}` → **200 with body** |
| Group | `POST /api/v1/groups` (create + map), `PUT \| DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}/external-ref` | `GET /api/v1/groups?external_id=…` | create and map only — an existing group is never changed |

Every resource above exposes `external_ref` (`integration`, `external_id`, `content_hash`, `last_synced_at`) or `null`.

The upsert answers **201** when it created a resource and **200** when it updated the already mapped one.

Groups work differently, and on purpose. `POST /api/v1/groups` **creates** a group — with an optional `external_id`, so an ERP project number becomes a group and its mapping in one call — but nothing in v1 ever **changes** an existing group: no rename, no type or visibility switch, no membership, no delete. That is why there is no `PUT /api/v1/groups/by-external-id`, and why calling `POST /api/v1/groups` twice creates twice. The `type_slug` field takes a locale-independent slug, and the set is tenant-specific: ask `GET /api/v1/groups/types` for the slugs this tenant accepts (`groups:read` is enough) instead of guessing them. Do not confuse it with the response's `type`, which is the translated label and cannot be sent back.

### Reading a resource back by your own id

There is no separate `by-external-id` **GET**: the read path is the `?external_id=` filter on the index endpoints above, and it answers with a **collection**, not with a single object. Since `integration + external_id` is unique per tenant, `data` holds exactly one entry or none — read `data[0]`, and treat `"data": []` as "nothing is mapped to this id yet, go ahead and create it". That is the normal answer, not an error; there is no 404 on this path. A token without an integration slug gets **422**.

Careful with the encoding here: the id sits in the **query string**, not in the body, so slashes, spaces and umlauts have to be percent-encoded — `ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx` is requested as `?external_id=ordner%2F%C3%9Cnterlagen%202026.docx`.

An empty answer is no proof that the id is free. The index hides soft-deleted resources, archived tasks and everything outside the token account's group visibility, so an id can be taken by something you cannot see — that is the **409** on the upsert. Only the upsert answers the question reliably.

### Which id to pick

`external_id` is a **required field in the request body** — the same place the group endpoint takes it — not a path segment. Kibi never interprets it, so anything your source system uses is fine: a SharePoint item id (`01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP`), a Jira key (`PROJ-4711`), a numeric primary key (`12345t62124`), a file path (`docs/guides/setup.md`). Because it sits in the body, slashes, spaces and umlauts need no URL encoding — `ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx` goes over the wire as it is.

The one rule: **pick an id that does not change when the object is renamed or moved.** A path is the tempting choice and the wrong one — move the file one folder up and the next sync no longer recognises what it wrote last week, so it creates a second resource and the first goes stale. Where the source system has an opaque id (SharePoint, Jira, most databases), use that and keep the path in the title or the content.

### What you have to know before you build this

- **Results are filtered by what the token's account can see.** Wiki pages, tasks and posts bound to a group are invisible to a token whose owner is not a member — and they are missing *silently*. No role lifts this. For a complete sync, put that account into every relevant group.
- **409 means the external id is taken** — tenant-wide, across entity types, possibly by something the token cannot see. A retry never helps; a different id does.
- **A soft-deleted resource keeps its mapping for 30 days.** Writing to the same external id within that window **restores** the resource with its history and comments (**200**). After the daily garbage collection force-deletes it, the same request creates a new one (**201**). Restoring tasks needs `tasks.update.any`; for wiki pages and posts, update permission is enough.
- **`notify: false`** on the upsert suppresses the announcement to all users. It matters for **posts** (on create and on update); wiki pages and tasks send no announcement anyway, so the flag is accepted there but does nothing. It never silences `@mention` notifications or webhooks.
- **Conflict detection is opt-in.** Send `If-Unmodified-Since` with the `Last-Modified` value from your last single-resource read or write and a write that would overwrite a meanwhile-changed resource is refused with **412**. Listings carry no such header — take `updated_at` from the entry there. Without the header the write is unconditional. Sending the header to an endpoint that does not evaluate it answers **400** rather than ignoring it silently. An HTTP date is second-precise, so a change within the same second as your read is not caught.
- **Break the sync loop with `origin`.** Every webhook payload carries `origin: {source, integration}`; skip any delivery whose `integration` is your own slug. It is the only guard that also works for deletes. See the webhook documentation for the event reference and signature verification.
- **Rate limits:** 30 writes per minute and 500 per hour; 120 reads per minute and 5000 per hour. Plan a bulk import around the hourly write budget.

`content_format` lets you send and read HTML or Markdown instead of the TipTap JSON described below — see the parameter documentation on each endpoint.

## Rich Text Content Format (TipTap JSON)

The `body` (posts) and `content` (wiki) fields use **TipTap JSON** — a structured document format.
You can also send a plain text string, which will be auto-wrapped in a basic paragraph.

### Document Structure

Every document is a `{"type": "doc", "content": [...]}` object containing an array of block nodes.

### Block Nodes

| Type | Description | Key Attributes |
|------|------------|----------------|
| `paragraph` | Text paragraph | `textAlign` |
| `heading` | Section heading | `level` (1-3) |
| `bulletList` | Unordered list (contains `listItem` nodes) | — |
| `orderedList` | Ordered list (contains `listItem` nodes) | — |
| `blockquote` | Quoted text block | — |
| `codeBlock` | Code snippet | `language` |
| `table` | Table with `tableRow`, `tableHeader`, `tableCell` | `colspan`, `rowspan` |
| `callout` | Info/warning/danger box | `type` (`info`, `warning`, `danger`) |
| `details` | Collapsible section (`detailsSummary` + `detailsContent`) | — |
| `stepList` | Numbered step-by-step guide (contains `stepItem` nodes) | — |
| `gridBuilder` | Multi-column layout (contains `gridBuilderColumn` nodes) | `data-cols`, `data-stack-at` |
| `seeAlso` | Related page links | `pages` (array of `{ulid, title}`) |
| `imageResize` | Image with sizing | `src`, `alt`, `containerStyle` |

### Inline Marks

Text nodes support `marks` for formatting:

| Mark | Example |
|------|---------|
| `bold` | `{"type": "text", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}], "text": "important"}` |
| `italic` | `{"type": "text", "marks": [{"type": "italic"}], "text": "note"}` |
| `code` | `{"type": "text", "marks": [{"type": "code"}], "text": "config"}` |
| `link` | `{"type": "text", "marks": [{"type": "link", "attrs": {"href": "https://..."}}], "text": "click"}` |

### Minimal Example

```json
{
  "type": "doc",
  "content": [
    {"type": "heading", "attrs": {"level": 1}, "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "Title"}]},
    {"type": "paragraph", "content": [
      {"type": "text", "text": "Hello "},
      {"type": "text", "marks": [{"type": "bold"}], "text": "world"}
    ]},
    {"type": "callout", "attrs": {"type": "info"}, "content": [
      {"type": "paragraph", "content": [{"type": "text", "text": "This is a note."}]}
    ]}
  ]
}
```

## Syncing an external system with Kibi (REST API v1)

This guide is for the case where the master data does **not** live in Kibi: pages
in OneDrive or SharePoint, Markdown files in a Git repository, issues in a
forge. Kibi is the frontend your people use; the other system stays the source
of truth, or both sides write and the two have to be reconciled.

The mechanism is a **mapping**: every wiki page, task, post, calendar event and
group can carry one identifier per integration — the path of the file, the item
id, the issue number. You write against that identifier and never have to keep a
table of Kibi ULIDs on your side.

Everything below is REST API v1 (`/api/v1`), bearer-token authenticated. The
interactive endpoint reference lives at `/docs/api` on your tenant.

---

### 1. The two things you need to understand first

#### The mapping

One row per (resource, integration) in `external_references`. Two uniqueness
rules apply, and both will bite you at some point:

- **`(integration, external_id)`** — an external id is used **once per
  integration, across the whole tenant and across all entity types**. The same
  `docs/setup.md` cannot be a wiki page and a task at the same time.
- **`(resource, integration)`** — a resource carries at most one id per
  integration. Writing a second one replaces the first.

Different integrations are independent: a page can be `docs/setup.md` for
`github` and `01ABC…` for `sharepoint` at the same time.

#### The integration slug

The slug is **not** part of any payload. It is read from the API token
(`App\Support\Api\IntegrationContext`). That is the whole isolation model: a
token *is* an integration, and it can only ever see and write its own mappings.

- Chosen **when the token is minted**, under **My profile > Integrations**.
- Only a **system administrator** can set it — the field is not even offered to
  anyone else, and sending it anyway is rejected.
- **Immutable.** There is no update endpoint for a token. A different slug means
  a different token.
- Format: `^[a-z0-9]+(-[a-z0-9]+)*$`, at most 64 characters — `github`,
  `ms-entra`, `sharepoint-docs`.
- A token **without** a slug gets **422** from every endpoint that needs one, and
  reads back `external_ref: null` everywhere rather than someone else's mapping.

> **The slug is a permission, not a label.** Whoever holds a token with the slug
> `github` may work on every `github` mapping in the tenant — including
> `DELETE /groups/{group}/external-ref` on a group they are not allowed to see.
> That exemption is deliberate (see [section 8](#8-deleting)), and it is why the
> field is restricted to system administrators.

---

### 2. What can be mapped

| Resource | Read the mapping | Filter | Write through | Delete |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Wiki page | `external_ref` on `GET /wiki`, `GET /wiki/{ulid}` | `?external_id=` | `PUT /wiki/by-external-id` | `DELETE /wiki/{ulid}` → 204 |
| Task | `external_ref` on `GET /tasks`, `GET /tasks/{ulid}` | `?external_id=` | `PUT /tasks/by-external-id` | `DELETE /tasks/{ulid}` → 204 |
| Post | `external_ref` on `GET /posts`, `GET /posts/{ulid}` | `?external_id=` | `PUT /posts/by-external-id` | `DELETE /posts/{ulid}` → **200 with body** |
| Calendar event | `external_ref` on `GET /calendar/events`, `GET /calendar/events/{ulid}` | `?external_id=` | `PUT /calendar/events/by-external-id` | `DELETE /calendar/events/{ulid}` → **200 with body** |
| Group | `external_ref` on `GET /groups`, `GET /groups/{ulid}` | `?external_id=` | `POST /groups` (create + map), `PUT /groups/{group}/external-ref` (map an existing one) | `DELETE /groups/{group}/external-ref` → 204 |

`external_ref` is `null` when the resource carries no mapping for **your**
integration, and otherwise:

```json
"external_ref": {
  "integration": "github",
  "external_id": "docs/guides/setup.md",
  "content_hash": "9f2b…",
  "last_synced_at": "2026-09-01T09:14:22+02:00"
}
```

**Groups are still the odd one out, but less than they were.** A sync can
**create** a group — `POST /groups`, see [section 4a](#4a-creating-a-group) — and
it can map an existing one. What it cannot do is **change** one: renaming,
switching the type or the visibility, archiving, deleting and membership all
stay in Kibi. Those are the levers that decide who sees what, and they are not
something a sync token should be able to move. There is consequently no
`PUT /groups/by-external-id`: `POST /groups` creates, and calling it twice
creates twice (or answers 409, if you sent the same external id both times).
`PUT /groups/{group}/external-ref` writes the mapping row and nothing else; the
group object is not touched.

**Calendar events differ in two ways** from wiki pages, tasks and posts, both
covered below: the schedule (`name`, `day`, and `start_time` or `full_day`) is
required on **every** upsert including updates ([section 4](#4-step-2--the-first-import)),
and a deleted event never comes back — it has no bin, so its mapping goes with
it and the external id is released immediately ([section 8](#8-step-6--deleting)).

> **Send a `type`, or nobody will see the events.** An event without one is
> created as `personal`, which is visible to its creator and to invited
> participants only — so a mirrored team calendar lands in the token owner's
> account and nowhere else. Send `type: "general"` for something everyone
> should see, or `type: "group"` together with `group_id`. The same rule holds
> for updates: only the account that **created** an event may write it, so a
> sync can update the events it imported itself but never one a person made in
> Kibi.

#### Choosing an external id

`external_id` is a **required field in the request body** on all five write
endpoints — the same place the group endpoint has always taken it, never a path
segment. That is the whole reason it moved: an id in the body needs no URL
encoding, so slashes, spaces and umlauts survive untouched.
`ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx` goes over the wire exactly as written.

Kibi never interprets the value, so anything the source system uses is a valid
id:

| Source system | A good `external_id` |
|---|---|
| SharePoint / OneDrive (Graph) | the item id — `01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP` |
| Jira | the issue key — `PROJ-4711` |
| A database of your own | the primary key — `12345t62124` |
| A Git repository | the file path — `docs/guides/setup.md` |
| A forge's issues | `repo/issues/42` |

**The one rule: pick an id that does not change when the object is renamed or
moved.** This is where syncs actually go wrong. A path is the tempting choice
and usually the wrong one — move the file one folder up and the next run no
longer recognises the page it wrote last week: it creates a second one, and the
first goes stale with nothing pointing at it. Where the source system has an
opaque id (SharePoint, Jira, most databases), address the object by that id and
carry the path in the title or the content, where it is allowed to change.

A Git repository is the honest exception: the path *is* the identity there, and
there is nothing more stable to use. Accept that a `git mv` shows up in Kibi as
a new page plus an orphan, and delete the orphan on your side.

---

### 3. Step 1 — mint the token

A system administrator opens **My profile > Integrations > Create token** and
sets:

- **Name** — free text, for humans.
- **Scopes** — `wiki:read`, `wiki:write`, `tasks:read`, `tasks:write`,
  `posts:read`, `posts:write`, `calendar:read`, `calendar:write`, `groups:read`,
  `groups:write`. Take only what the sync needs.
- **Integration slug** — `github`, `sharepoint`, whatever names your side.

The plaintext token is shown **once**. There is no way to retrieve it later and
no way to change the slug afterwards.

```bash
export TOKEN='kibi_…'
export BASE='https://acme.kibi.de/api/v1'
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$BASE/wiki?limit=1"
```

#### The account behind the token matters more than you think

A token belongs to the account that minted it, and **every request is filtered
by what that account can see.** Wiki pages, tasks and posts bound to a group are
invisible to a token whose owner is not in that group — and they are invisible
**silently**: the list is simply shorter. Nothing in the response says
"3 records were filtered out". From the outside that looks exactly like data
loss on the Kibi side.

This is not a role question. Holding SYSTEM_ADMIN does not lift the filter; the
visibility scope runs on the query regardless of role. **If the sync is meant to
cover everything, put the token's account into every relevant group** — and
re-check that after someone creates a new private group.

---

### 4. Step 2 — the first import

Write each source object to its external id. `PUT` is the only verb you need:
**201** when nothing was mapped to that id yet, **200** when the mapped resource
was updated.

```bash
curl -s -X PUT "$BASE/wiki/by-external-id" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "external_id": "01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP",
        "title": "Setup",
        "content": "## Setup\n\nRead this first.",
        "content_format": "markdown",
        "notify": false
      }'
```

Four things about the payload:

- **`external_id` is a required body field**, not a path segment — see
  [Choosing an external id](#choosing-an-external-id) for what to put in it.
- **Omitted fields stay untouched.** Leaving out `content` keeps the stored
  content; sending an empty string does the same. There is no way to clear a
  field by omission. The one exception is the calendar event's schedule: `name`,
  `day` and either `start_time` or `full_day: true` are required on every call,
  update included. An event *is* its point in time, and the create branch has no
  earlier state to fall back on.
- **`content_format`** picks the wire format — `json` (TipTap, the default for
  wiki and posts), `html` or `markdown`. Tasks default to `html`. Calendar
  events take **no** `content_format` at all: their `description` is plain text
  on the way in and the stored HTML on the way out, as it has been since v1
  shipped. Read
  [content-formats.md](content-formats.md) before you choose; the short version
  is that **HTML is not fully lossless** (a handful of node types — mentions,
  the "see also" widget, emoticon/voice/hurdle nodes — flatten on the way
  through) and **Markdown loses considerably more**
  (everything Markdown has no syntax for: tables, callouts, step lists, grids).
  Use HTML if your system speaks it, Markdown only when the other side owns the
  content anyway, JSON when Kibi is the source of truth.
- **`notify: false`** on a bulk import. See below.

#### `notify`

Defaults to `true`. It exists for the first import, where a few hundred
resources arriving at once should not announce themselves to the whole
workforce.

Where it actually does something today:

| Endpoint | Effect of `notify: false` |
|---|---|
| `PUT /posts/by-external-id` | **Real.** Suppresses the announcement to all users — on create *and* on update, including the update that follows a restore. |
| `PUT /wiki/by-external-id` | None. Wiki pages send no announcement on creation. |
| `PUT /tasks/by-external-id` | None. Tasks created here send no announcement. |
| `PUT /calendar/events/by-external-id` | None. The endpoint assigns neither participants nor external guests, so nobody is invited and nobody is notified. |

It is accepted on all four so the payload is the same shape everywhere; on wiki,
tasks and calendar events it is a no-op you can leave in.

What `notify: false` does **not** silence, even on posts: people named with an
`@mention` in the body still get their notification (that message is addressed to
a person, not to the workforce), and webhook subscribers still receive
`post.created` / `post.updated`.

#### Budget the import against the rate limit

| | Per minute | Per hour |
|---|---|---|
| Reads, any token | 120 | 5000 |
| Writes, **token with an integration slug** | 120 | 3000 |
| Writes, personal token (no slug) | 30 | 500 |

A token that carries an integration slug gets the larger write budget because it
is a machine, and because only a system administrator can issue one. An import
of 2000 objects runs in about 17 minutes on it. On a personal token the same
import takes at least four hours.

Expect `429` with a `Retry-After` when you exceed either limit. The minute limit
is there to absorb a burst — a batch your side flushes at once; the hour limit is
what bounds a sync that has gone into a loop.

The counter is keyed by the **token**, so two integrations calling from the same
egress address get a bucket each and neither can lock the other out. Requests
that arrive without a valid token — a wrong or revoked one included — fall back
to a per-IP bucket, which is what keeps guessing at tokens capped.

> Two things changed on 2026-09-01, both of which make the numbers above
> larger than what you actually got before:
>
> - The counter used to be keyed by IP for everyone — the limiter ran before the
>   token was resolved, so the fallback applied to every request.
> - Every `/api/v1` request also passed a second, older limiter of **60 per
>   minute per IP**, which was the smaller and therefore the effective number.
>   The 120 reads per minute documented here were never reachable. That limiter
>   no longer applies to v1.
>
> If you paced an import around either, you can go faster now.

#### Groups have a second budget, and it is not the rate limit

`POST /groups` ([section 4a](#4a-creating-a-group)) is the one write in this API
where the rate limit is not the binding constraint. Every group creation
invalidates the tenant's cache — and not just the group's own entries: the cache
is tag-based, and flushing one tag flushes the tenant's whole cache with it.
Creating a group therefore empties the cache for **everyone working in that
tenant at that moment**, and every page they open afterwards rebuilds from the
database.

One group is nothing. Three hundred groups fired back to back inside the 3000/h
write budget is a tenant that spends the whole import with a cold cache, which
people notice as a platform that has become slow for no visible reason.

**So pace group creation deliberately, not against the rate limit.** Spread it
over the run — a short pause between groups, or a batch per interval — and
where you can, put it outside working hours. This is the one endpoint where
staying under the limit is not enough.

None of the other write endpoints behave this way; for wiki pages, tasks, posts
and calendar events the rate limit really is the only ceiling.

---

### 4a. Creating a group

Groups are the one entity a sync can bring into existence but never change. The
case this is built for: a project number in the ERP should become a group in
Kibi, and the project number is the external id.

```bash
curl -s -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "name": "Neubau Halle 4",
        "type_slug": "project",
        "description": "Projektgruppe zur Baustelle in Rheine.",
        "external_id": "P-2026-0815"
      }' \
  "$BASE/groups"
```

**201** with the group, `external_ref` included. Fields:

| Field | | |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | required | |
| `type_slug` | optional | a **slug**, see below. Defaults to `miscellaneous`. |
| `description` | optional | plain text, or a TipTap document |
| `visibility` | optional | `all` (default) or `members` |
| `external_id` | optional | your own id; creates the mapping in the same call |

Everything else a group can have — cover image, location, templates, the tool
list, membership — is deliberately not here. A sync does not need it, and each
of those would be a second way to configure a group next to Kibi itself.

The ERP project number is a textbook `external_id` by the rule in
[Choosing an external id](#choosing-an-external-id): it is assigned once and
survives every rename of the project. Renaming the group in Kibi does not touch
it either, so the mapping holds in both directions.

Also see the pacing note in
[section 4](#groups-have-a-second-budget-and-it-is-not-the-rate-limit) before
you import a few hundred of these — group creation is the one write in this API
where the rate limit is not the binding constraint.

#### Ask for the types, do not guess them

`type_slug` takes a locale-independent **slug**, and the set is not fixed: next to
the six standard types every tenant has, a tenant can define its own. There is
no way to guess those, which is what `GET /groups/types` is for:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$BASE/groups/types"
```

```json
{
  "data": [
    { "value": "department", "label": "Abteilung", "standard": true },
    { "value": "project",    "label": "Projekt",   "standard": true },
    { "value": "baustelle",  "label": "Baustelle", "standard": false }
  ]
}
```

`standard: false` marks a type this tenant added for itself. Every `value` in
the list is accepted by `type_slug`; anything else is a **422**. The endpoint needs
`groups:read` only.

Two of the standard types are HR-managed — `department` and `location`. They are
listed for everyone, but creating a group with one of them needs a token whose
account may manage them, and otherwise answers 422. A mirror of an ERP wants
`project` anyway. The same applies to `visibility: "members"`: introducing it
takes a token that may manage groups.

API v1 cannot create a *type*. A slug that is missing from the list has to be
added once by a system administrator in Kibi before the sync can use it.

> **`type_slug` on both sides; `type` is display only.** The field you send is
> `type_slug`, and the slug you sent comes back under the same name. `type` in
> the response is the label a person sees, translated into the tenant's
> language — `"Projekt"`, not `"project"` — so it cannot be sent back.
>
> `POST /groups` does still accept the slug under `type`, the name the endpoint
> first shipped with. It is deprecated, it means exactly `type_slug`, and
> `type_slug` wins when both are sent. Do not build on it.

#### It is a create, not an upsert

Calling it twice creates two groups. There is no `PUT /groups/by-external-id`,
because that endpoint would have to *update* a group on the second call, and
updating groups is exactly what stays out of v1. If your sync may run against
groups it wrote earlier, ask first:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$BASE/groups?external_id=P-2026-0815"
```

An empty `data` means nothing is mapped to that id — but see
[section 5](#an-empty-answer-is-not-proof-the-id-is-free): the honest answer
comes from the **409**. If you send an `external_id` that is already taken, no
group is created at all; the group row and its mapping are written in one
transaction, so a lost race leaves nothing behind.

`external_id` is optional here — leave it out and you get a group with no
mapping, which is also the only case where the endpoint works on a token
**without** an integration slug. With an id and without a slug the answer is
**422**, and no group is created.

#### What creating a group sets off

More than a row in a table, and a bulk import should know it:

- **The token's own account joins the group as administrator.** Not a side
  effect to work around — it is what keeps the group visible to the sync
  afterwards, since every read is filtered by what that account can see
  ([section 3](#the-account-behind-the-token-matters-more-than-you-think)). It
  is also the answer to the visibility problem that section raises: for groups
  the sync created itself, you never have to remember to add the account
  anywhere.

  The flip side is worth stating plainly: **the account accumulates one such
  membership per created group.** After 300 project groups it administers 300
  groups, it appears in each of their member lists, and it receives whatever a
  group administrator receives. That is correct behaviour, not a leak — but if
  you were expecting a machine account that stays out of everybody's way, this
  is where it does not.
- A **group chat** and a **file folder** are created for the group.
- If the tenant switched on *notify administrators about new groups*, every
  system administrator is notified — **once per group**. There is no flag on the
  endpoint to suppress this (unlike `notify` on the post upsert): it is a tenant
  setting, and it is off unless somebody turned it on. Check it before importing
  a few hundred groups — that is a few hundred notifications per administrator.
- **Every creation flushes the tenant's cache.** This is the constraint that
  actually bites on a bulk import, and it has its own note in
  [section 4](#groups-have-a-second-budget-and-it-is-not-the-rate-limit): staying
  under the rate limit is not enough, spread the creates out.

### 5. Step 3 — reading back

This is the read counterpart to the upsert: *give me the resource I know under
my own id*. There is no separate endpoint for it — the index endpoints take
`?external_id=` as a filter:

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/wiki?external_id=01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP"
```

The filter applies to all five index endpoints and **requires a token with a
slug** — without one it is 422, not an empty result.

Reading back by your own id is the lookup. For the sweep — *everything that
changed since T* — see `updated_since` below.

#### It answers with a collection, not with one object

`integration + external_id` is unique across the tenant, so the list holds at
most one entry — but it is still a list, and your code has to read `data[0]`:

```json
{ "data": [ { "id": "01j8x…", "title": "Setup", "external_ref": { … } } ] }
```

Nothing mapped to that id looks like this — **not** a 404:

```json
{ "data": [] }
```

An empty `data` is the normal, expected answer for "I have not written this
object to Kibi yet", and the right reaction is to create it with the upsert.
Do not treat it as an error.

#### The id goes in the query string, so encode it

This is the one place where the encoding problem the upsert no longer has still
applies. A query parameter carrying slashes, spaces or umlauts has to be
percent-encoded:

```bash
# external_id = ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/wiki?external_id=ordner%2F%C3%9Cnterlagen%202026.docx"
```

Most HTTP clients do this for you if you pass the value as a query parameter
rather than pasting it into the URL string — use that path and the question does
not come up.

#### `updated_since` — the catch-up scan

The other way to read back: *what changed since I last looked?* Every index
endpoint takes `?updated_since=` with an ISO 8601 moment, and answers with the
records whose `updated_at` is at or after it.

```bash
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "$BASE/wiki?updated_since=2026-09-01T00:00:00%2B00:00&sort=updated_at&limit=50"
```

This is the filter you need when webhooks were down and a full re-scan is the
only way back. It is deliberately about the **change** date, not the creation
date: a page written last year and edited this morning comes back, which is
exactly the record a creation-date filter would miss and exactly the one your
sync is missing.

The comparison is **inclusive**, and the stored timestamps are second-precision.
The record sitting exactly on your watermark therefore arrives once more on the
next run. That is at-least-once, on purpose — the alternative would drop every
change that happened in the same second as your watermark. Writing it through
the upsert again costs nothing.

#### `sort=updated_at` — walk the pages and move the watermark

Every index endpoint keeps the order it always had: `created_at` descending for
wiki pages and tasks, `published_at` descending for posts, `name` for groups,
`day` + `start_time` for calendar events. `?sort=updated_at` switches to
**least recently changed first** — ascending, the other way round from every
default here.

That direction is the point. A catch-up scan works the oldest changes first, so
after each page it can move its watermark to the last `updated_at` it saw and
resume there if it dies halfway. Descending, it would have to finish every page
before it could record anything.

Both orders now break ties on the record id. Without that, two records carrying
the same second — the normal case after a bulk import — could swap places
between two queries, so page 1 returned a record and page 2 returned it again
while another was never shown at all. Postgres makes no promise about the order
of equal rows, and the scan silently lost data.

An unknown `sort` value is a **422**, not a silent fallback: a caller who
believed they had re-sorted would advance a watermark against the wrong order.

The response shape is unchanged — `data`, `links`, `meta` with `total` and
`last_page`, the same offset pagination as before.

#### An empty answer is not proof the id is free

**The index is not an existence check.** It never returns soft-deleted
resources, `GET /tasks` additionally excludes archived tasks, and everything
outside the token account's group visibility is missing silently. An external id
can be taken by something the list does not show you — which is exactly the 409
described in [section 6](#6-step-4--the-ongoing-inbound-sync-external--kibi).
The upsert is the only reliable answer to "is this id taken?"; it looks through
soft-deletes on purpose.

### 6. Step 4 — the ongoing inbound sync (external → Kibi)

Exactly the same `PUT` as the import, without `notify: false`. Nothing else
changes: 201 for new, 200 for existing, omitted fields untouched.

#### 409 — the external id is taken

**A retry never helps.** 409 means `(your slug, that external id)` is already
mapped, to something you cannot see or to a different entity type. The resource
behind it is neither revealed nor modified — visibility wins over uniqueness.

Your options are: pick a different external id, or — if the mapping in the way
is one your own integration holds — release it first:

| Entity | Unlink |
|---|---|
| Wiki page | `DELETE /api/v1/wiki/{ulid}/external-ref` |
| Task | `DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{ulid}/external-ref` |
| Post | `DELETE /api/v1/posts/{ulid}/external-ref` |
| Group | `DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}/external-ref` |
| Calendar event | none needed — see below |

Calendar events need no unlink endpoint: they have no bin, so deleting one
releases its external id at once.

See *Releasing a mapping* below for what these endpoints do and do not touch.

#### 412 — someone edited it in Kibi meanwhile

Wiki pages are edited collaboratively in the browser. A page can be open in
somebody's editor while your sync writes over it. To prevent that:

1. Take the `Last-Modified` value from your last single-resource read
   (`GET /wiki/{ulid}`, `/tasks/{ulid}`, `/posts/{ulid}`,
   `/calendar/events/{ulid}`) or from your previous write to that resource. From
   a listing, take the entry's `updated_at` and convert it to an HTTP date.
2. Send it as `If-Unmodified-Since` on the next write.
3. **412** means it changed in the meantime; nothing was written. Re-read, merge,
   retry.

```bash
curl -s -X PUT "$BASE/wiki/by-external-id" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H 'If-Unmodified-Since: Wed, 21 Oct 2026 07:28:00 GMT' \
  -d '{"external_id": "01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP", "title": "Setup", "content": "…", "content_format": "markdown"}'
```

Four things worth knowing:

- **Without the header, the write is unconditional.** That is the pre-existing
  behaviour of API v1 and it is kept deliberately. Conflict detection is opt-in.
- **Only some endpoints evaluate it** — the eight `by-external-id` and `{id}`
  update routes for wiki, tasks, posts and calendar events. Sending the header
  at any **other** write endpoint answers **400** and writes
  nothing. That is on purpose: a silently ignored header would let you believe
  you were protected when you were not.
- **`Last-Modified` comes back on single-resource reads and on writes, not on
  listings.** `GET /wiki/{ulid}` and its three siblings carry the header, as
  does every write that evaluates the precondition. A listing — including the
  `?external_id=` read-back — does not: a page of results has no single
  timestamp, and the newest one on the page would be a licence to overwrite the
  older entries. Use `updated_at` from the entry there.
- **Second granularity.** An HTTP date has no sub-second precision, so an edit
  that lands in the *same second* as your read slips through undetected. This is
  inherent to the mechanism, not a bug that will be fixed.

An unparseable date is **400**, not a silent pass.

### 7. Step 5 — the ongoing outbound sync (Kibi → external)

Subscribe to webhooks. The full guide — enabling the feature, creating the
endpoint, verifying the HMAC signature, the retry policy and the complete event
list — is [webhooks.md](webhooks.md). The events relevant to a sync are
`wiki_page.created/updated/deleted`, `task.created/updated/completed/assigned`
and `post.created/updated/deleted`.

#### Break the loop

Your write into Kibi produces a webhook. If your receiver treats it as a change
and writes back, the two systems ping-pong forever.

**Every webhook payload carries `origin`:**

```json
"origin": { "source": "api", "integration": "github" }
```

`source` is `"api"` for a change that came in through API v1 with a token and
`"ui"` for everything else (a person in Kibi, a job, a console command).
`integration` is the slug of the token that made the write, or `null`.

Ignore any delivery where `origin.integration` is your own slug:

```js
if (payload.data.origin?.integration === 'github') return res.status(200).send('own write');
```

That is the reliable guard, and it is the **only** one that works for deletes —
a delete has no content to compare.

`content_hash` on the mapping is a secondary signal: it holds the SHA-256 of the
content Kibi stored at your last write through the API. If it is unchanged
between two reads, nothing was written through your integration since. Note that
recomputing the hash on your side means reproducing Kibi's normalisation
(recursive key sorting before serialisation) — do not build your loop protection
on that. Use `origin`.

Two more things about webhooks that matter for a sync, both detailed in
[webhooks.md](webhooks.md): **order is not guaranteed** (reorder on
`X-Kibi-Timestamp` if you depend on it), and a receiver that takes longer than
10 seconds counts as a failed attempt.

### 8. Step 6 — deleting

| Endpoint | Answer |
|---|---|
| `DELETE /api/v1/wiki/{ulid}` | **204**, no body |
| `DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{ulid}` | **204**, no body |
| `DELETE /api/v1/posts/{ulid}` | **200** with `{"message": "Post deleted successfully."}` |
| `DELETE /api/v1/calendar/events/{ulid}` | **200** with `{"message": "Calendar event deleted successfully."}` |
| `DELETE /api/v1/wiki/{ulid}/external-ref` | **204**, no body — mapping only |
| `DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{ulid}/external-ref` | **204**, no body — mapping only |
| `DELETE /api/v1/posts/{ulid}/external-ref` | **204**, no body — mapping only |
| `DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}/external-ref` | **204**, no body — mapping only |

The post and calendar endpoints are inconsistent with the other two and stay
that way: they predate them, and changing their status code would break every
integration already reading that body. Handle both.

Wiki, task and post deletes are **soft** deletes. A wiki page with subpages is
refused with **422** — move or delete the children first.

#### The calendar event is the exception: it is deleted for good

A calendar event has **no bin**. `DELETE /calendar/events/{ulid}` removes the
row, and the mapping goes with it — the external id is free again **at once**.
Writing to that id afterwards creates a brand-new event and answers **201**, with
a new ULID and no history.

Everything in the next section is therefore about wiki pages, tasks and posts
only. For calendar events there is no 30-day window and nothing to restore: a
delete is final, and re-importing the same source appointment produces a
different event.

#### For the other three, the mapping survives a delete, for 30 days

This is the single most consequential detail on this page.

A soft-deleted resource **keeps** its mapping. Writing to the same external id
again therefore does not create a duplicate — it **restores** the resource with
its history and comments and updates it, answering **200**.

A daily garbage collector force-deletes what has been in the bin for more than
**30 days** — `kibi:garbage-collect-wiki-content`, `…-posts`, `…-tasks` and
`…-groups`, one per mappable entity, all with the same window. A force-delete
takes the mapping with it and releases the external id.

So the same request has two different outcomes depending on when it arrives:

| A source file comes back… | Result |
|---|---|
| within 30 days of the delete | **200** — the original page is restored, history and comments intact |
| after 30 days | **201** — a brand-new page, no history, no comments, new ULID |

Restoring is checked as a permission of its own, but on all three resource types
it now asks the same question as `update`: whoever may update the resource may
bring it back. A token that may write a resource can therefore always restore
it.

> Until 2026-09-01 tasks were the exception: restoring one required
> `tasks.update.any`, a manager permission, so a token that could update its own
> tasks got **403** on the restore and the restore path was unusable for a
> normal integration.

#### Releasing a mapping

Every mappable entity has an unlink endpoint, and they all behave the same way:

```
DELETE /api/v1/wiki/{ulid}/external-ref
DELETE /api/v1/tasks/{ulid}/external-ref
DELETE /api/v1/posts/{ulid}/external-ref
DELETE /api/v1/groups/{group}/external-ref
```

All answer **204** and remove **only** the mapping your token's integration
holds. The resource is not touched — not deleted, not restored, not changed, not
even its `updated_at`. A `sharepoint` mapping on the same resource survives a
call from a `github` token untouched.

**This is the way out of an external id you picked wrong.** The classic case:
your integration keyed on file paths, found out — as this guide warns — that a
rename breaks that, and now wants to move to stable item ids. Without an unlink
the old ids stay taken until the resource leaves the bin 30 days later, and every
attempt to reuse one answers 409.

These endpoints also reach a resource that has become **invisible since you
wrote the mapping** — soft-deleted, moved into a group you are not in, set back
to draft, or switched to members-only — and they reach it for exactly one
reason: to release the external id. The resource stays deleted, stays invisible,
is not restored and is not revealed. Without that exemption its external id would
stay blocked tenant-wide with no way out short of a database intervention.
**Holding the mapping is the permission to release it** — your integration wrote
that row itself, and had to pass the visibility check to do so.

They are idempotent: a resource with no mapping for your integration also answers
204. But if there was nothing to delete **and** you cannot see the resource, you
get the same refusal its single read gives you — **404** for wiki pages, tasks
and posts, **403** for groups. The idempotent 204 must not become an existence
oracle for resources you cannot see.

### 9. Status codes on the sync endpoints

| Code | Meaning | Retry? |
|---|---|---|
| 200 | Existing resource updated (or restored and updated) | — |
| 201 | New resource created | — |
| 204 | Deleted / mapping removed | — |
| 400 | `If-Unmodified-Since` sent to an endpoint that does not evaluate it, or an unparseable date | No — fix the request |
| 403 | The token's account may not create/update/restore this resource. On calendar events this is the flat rule that only the creator may write one — so a sync can only update events its own token created | No |
| 404 | No resource with that ULID (or not visible to this token) | No |
| 409 | The external id is already taken in this integration | **Never** — use a different id |
| 412 | Changed since your `If-Unmodified-Since`; nothing written | Yes, after re-reading |
| 422 | Token has no integration slug, unknown `content_format`, unknown or HR-managed group `type_slug`, wiki page has subpages, validation | No — fix the request or the token |
| 429 | Rate limit; honour `Retry-After` | Yes, later |

#### `code` — branch on this, not on the message

The status alone does not say enough. Five unrelated things answer **422**, and
they ask for five different reactions: a new token, a code change on your side, a
corrected request, a business decision, a fixed field. Telling them apart used to
mean matching on an English sentence — and those sentences change whenever
somebody improves a wording.

Error responses therefore carry a `code` **next to** `message`:

```json
{
  "message": "This external id is already mapped to a resource you cannot see.",
  "code": "external_id_taken"
}
```

`message` is unchanged, word for word. **Branch on `code`, log `message`.** A
code is never renamed; if a case is ever split more finely, a new code appears
beside it.

| `code` | Status | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `external_id_taken` | 409 | `(your slug, that external id)` is already mapped, possibly to something you cannot see or to another entity type | Use a different id, or release your own mapping with `DELETE /{entity}/{ulid}/external-ref` |
| `integration_slug_missing` | 422 | The token carries no integration slug | Ask an administrator for a new token — the slug cannot be added later |
| `invalid_external_id` | 422 | `?external_id=` did not arrive as a plain string (typically `?external_id[]=…`) | Fix the query string |
| `unknown_content_format` | 422 | `format` / `content_format` is not one of `json`, `html`, `markdown` | Fix your client |
| `has_subpages` | 422 | The wiki page still has children and was not deleted | Move or delete the children first |
| `restore_forbidden` | 403 | The external id points at a deleted resource this account may not restore | Different account, or a different id |
| `precondition_failed` | 412 | The resource changed after your `If-Unmodified-Since`; nothing was written | Re-read, merge, retry |
| `conditional_write_unsupported` | 400 | You sent `If-Unmodified-Since` to an endpoint that does not evaluate it | Drop the header there |
| `invalid_http_date` | 400 | `If-Unmodified-Since` is not an RFC 9110 HTTP date | Send back the `Last-Modified` value verbatim |

**Two things carry no `code`, on purpose:**

- **Field validation.** A 422 out of the normal request validation already
  carries `errors` keyed by field name — more precise than any code could be.
  That format is untouched, and those responses have no `code`.
- **A plain 403 from a permission check, or a 404 for a resource that is not
  there.** At a single endpoint there is nothing to tell apart.

So: a `code` is present when this table lists one, and absent otherwise. Treat a
missing `code` as "fall back to the status".

### 10. The short list of things that catch people out

1. **A shorter list is not an empty database.** Group visibility filters silently
   and applies to every role. Put the token's account in the relevant groups.
2. **A path makes a bad external id.** It changes when the object is renamed or
   moved, and the next run then creates a second resource next to a stale one.
   Use the source system's opaque id where there is one.
3. **409 is never worth a retry.** The id is taken, possibly by something you
   cannot see or by a different entity type. If the mapping in the way is your
   own, `DELETE /{entity}/{ulid}/external-ref` releases it.
4. **The 30-day window changes what a re-import means** — restore before,
   fresh resource after. It does not apply to calendar events: those are deleted
   for good, and a re-import always makes a new one.
5. **`notify: false` only really does something for posts.**
6. **Without `If-Unmodified-Since` the API writes unconditionally**, and with it
   at an unsupported endpoint you get 400. Which of the two 400s it is, `code`
   tells you — branch on that, never on `message`. The wording is
   documentation; the code is the contract.
7. **`Last-Modified` comes back on single-resource reads and on writes**, never
   on a listing — there, read `updated_at`. And a re-scan wants `updated_since`
   together with `sort=updated_at`: without the sort you are paging over the
   creation order while records move underneath you, and you cannot advance a
   watermark until the last page is in.
8. **Use `origin`, not `content_hash`, for loop protection** — and note that a
   delete has nothing but `origin`.
9. **`DELETE /posts/{post}` and `DELETE /calendar/events/{event}` answer 200 with
   a body**, the newer deletes answer 204.
10. **The slug cannot be changed.** Wrong slug means a new token.
11. **Write budget depends on the slug** — 3000/hour with one, 500/hour without.
    A sync without a slug cannot use the by-external-id endpoints anyway, so if
    you are pacing an import against 500/hour, check the token first.
12. **`POST /groups` is not an upsert.** It creates, every time. And the group
    `type_slug` is a slug from `GET /groups/types`, never the label that comes
    back in `type`.
13. **Creating groups needs pacing beyond the rate limit.** Each one flushes the
    tenant's whole cache, so a burst of hundreds leaves everybody in that tenant
    on a cold cache for the length of the import. Spread them out.

## Content Formats (REST API v1)

Kibi stores rich text as a **TipTap document** — a nested JSON structure. If your
master data lives in GitHub (Markdown) or SharePoint (HTML), you do not have to
rebuild that structure. Ask for the format your system speaks, and send the
format your system already has.

### 1. The two parameters

| | Where | Field | Values |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Reading** | query string | `?format=` | `json`, `html`, `markdown` |
| **Writing** | request body | `content_format` | `json`, `html`, `markdown` |

Anything else is refused with **422** and nothing is written. Both parameters are
optional; leaving them out keeps the behaviour every existing integration
already sees.

### 2. Which endpoints, and what each one defaults to

| Resource | Field | Default | Endpoints |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wiki page | `content` | `json` | `GET/POST/PUT /api/v1/wiki…` |
| Post | `body` | `json` | `GET/POST/PUT /api/v1/posts…` |
| Task | `description` | **`html`** | `GET/POST/PUT /api/v1/tasks…` |

Tasks are the odd one out on purpose. `tasks.description` is an HTML column (the
mirror of the TipTap source in `description_json`), and API v1 has always
returned and accepted HTML there. Making `json` the default would have broken
every integration that already reads the field, so the default follows what the
resource has always been rather than being made uniform for its own sake.

Reading and writing are independent. `?format=` describes the response,
`content_format` describes the payload — a `PUT` may send Markdown and read the
result back as JSON in the same call.

### 3. What each format carries

Every format travels through HTML: Markdown is converted to HTML and then
parsed into a TipTap document, and back the same way. There is exactly one HTML
parser involved, the one that knows all of Kibi's custom nodes.

This table was **measured**, node by node, by taking a document through
`json → format → json` and comparing the node types that came back. It is not a
statement of intent.

| Node / mark | `json` | `html` | `markdown` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Headings, paragraphs, blockquote, horizontal rule | yes | yes | yes |
| Bullet / ordered lists | yes | yes | yes |
| Bold, italic, links, inline code | yes | yes | yes |
| Code blocks (incl. language) | yes | yes | yes |
| Images | yes | yes | yes (as `![alt](src)`) |
| Tables | yes | yes | **no** — cell text only |
| Callouts (info / tip / warning / important) | yes | yes | **no** — text only |
| Step lists, grids, details/accordion | yes | yes | **no** — text only |
| Task lists (checkboxes) | yes | yes | **no** — text only |
| Draw.io diagrams | yes | yes | **degraded** — plain image |
| YouTube, Vimeo, native video | yes | yes | **no** |
| Lead paragraph, checked list | yes | yes | **no** |
| Text alignment | yes | yes | **no** |
| Highlight, sub/superscript, colour | yes | yes | **no** |
| Resized images (`imageResize`) | yes | yes | **degraded** — plain image, size lost |
| Loom embeds | yes | yes | **no** — dropped |
| **Mentions** (`@name`) | yes | **no** — plain link | **no** |
| **"See also" widget** | yes | **no** — dropped | **no** |
| **Emoticons, voice placeholders, hurdles** | yes | **no** — dropped | **no** |

**JSON is exact.** It is what Kibi stores; nothing is translated. If you cannot
afford to lose anything, use JSON.

**HTML is lossless for almost everything, but not quite.** Most custom nodes
render with a marker attribute (`data-callout-type`, `data-drawio`,
`data-image-resize`, `data-loom-video`, `data-native-video`, …) and parse back
from it, so a callout that leaves as HTML comes back a callout. The rows in
bold above are the exceptions: those nodes have no HTML parser at all, so an
HTML roundtrip flattens them.

One caveat on resized images: the node, its `src` and its `width`/`height`
survive, but the first roundtrip copies the wrapper's `display: flex` onto the
image itself as an inline style. The second roundtrip no longer changes
anything — the drift is one-off, not cumulative.

> Until 2026-09-01 `imageResize` and `loom` were in the lossy group as well:
> both rendered their marker attribute as an empty string, and the renderer
> drops empty attributes, so the marker never reached the markup and the parse
> rule could not match. A resized image came back as an ordinary image, a Loom
> embed disappeared entirely.

**Markdown is a projection, not a representation.** Markdown has no syntax for a
callout, a step list, a grid or a table cell's structure, so those constructs
arrive as their plain text. This is deliberate and it is tested — see
`tests/Feature/Tenant/TipTap/ContentFormatRoundtripTest.php`, which pins both
the HTML roundtrip *and* the Markdown loss. The alternative — letting raw
`<div>` blocks ride along inside the Markdown — was rejected: those blocks come
back half-converted and reparse into structures the editor schema does not
allow. A clean loss beats a broken document.

**Use Markdown for content you own on the other side** (a Git repository is the
source, Kibi is the mirror). **Use JSON when Kibi is the source** and you need
the page back exactly as it was.

### 4. Examples

Read a wiki page as Markdown:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  "https://acme.kibi.de/api/v1/wiki/01J…?format=markdown"
```

```json
{ "data": { "id": "01J…", "content": "## Setup\n\nBitte **zuerst** lesen." } }
```

Mirror a Markdown file from a repository onto its mapped page:

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://acme.kibi.de/api/v1/wiki/by-external-id" \
  -d '{
        "external_id": "docs/setup.md",
        "title": "Setup",
        "content": "## Setup\n\nBitte **zuerst** lesen.",
        "content_format": "markdown"
      }'
```

Mirror an issue body onto a task, addressed by the tracker's own key — the
external id is whatever the source system calls the object, not necessarily a
path:

```bash
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  "https://acme.kibi.de/api/v1/tasks/by-external-id" \
  -d '{ "external_id": "PROJ-4711", "title": "Fix login",
        "description": "- [ ] reproduce\n- [ ] fix",
        "content_format": "markdown" }'
```

### 5. Two things that will trip you up

**A string field under a string format.** `content_format: html` or `markdown`
means the field is a **string**. Sending a TipTap object alongside it is a
contradiction and is refused with 422 rather than guessed at. The reverse holds
for tasks: `content_format: json` means `description` is an **object**.

**Omitting the field still means "leave it alone".** On the `by-external-id`
endpoints a missing `content` / `body` / `description` keeps the stored value,
whatever `content_format` says. Sending an empty string does the same — it is
not a way to clear the field.

### 6. Raw HTML inside Markdown

CommonMark lets raw HTML through, so `<img src=x onerror=…>` inside a Markdown
payload reaches Kibi as markup. It does not survive: everything written under
`markdown` (and under `html` for wiki pages and posts) is parsed into a TipTap
document, and that schema keeps only the attributes it knows about. Event
handlers, `<script>` and unknown tags are dropped at that point.

The one path that stores your markup verbatim is a **task** written with
`content_format: html` — `tasks.description` is an HTML column and API v1 has
always taken it as-is. That is unchanged behaviour, not something the formats
introduced, but it is worth knowing if you relay third-party content into it.

post.description:
Creates a group and, when you send an `external_id`, maps it to your own
object in the same call — the ERP project number that became this group,
for instance. That is the whole point of the endpoint: a sync writes
`P-2026-0815` once and finds the group again by that id forever after,
without keeping a table of Kibi ULIDs.

```bash
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: Bearer kbc_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"Neubau Halle 4","type_slug":"project","external_id":"P-2026-0815"}' \
  "https://<tenant>.kibi.de/api/v1/groups"
```

Answers **201** with the new group, including `external_ref` when an id
came along. `type_slug` takes a **slug** — ask `GET /api/v1/groups/types`
for the ones this tenant has, and expect a **422** for anything else. It
is the same field you read back as `type_slug`; the response's `type` is
the translated label for humans and cannot be sent back here.

Without `type_slug` the group becomes **`miscellaneous`**, and that default is
deliberate: `department` and `location` are HR-managed and need a
permission a sync token normally does not hold, so defaulting to either
would turn "I left the field out" into a 422 that only shows up in
production.

### What creating a group sets off

More than a row in a table, and a bulk import should know it:

- **The token's own account joins the group as administrator.** Not an
  accident — it is what keeps the group visible to the sync afterwards,
  because every read is filtered by what that account can see. The flip
  side: the account collects one such membership per import, so after 300
  project groups it administers 300 groups.
- A **group chat** and a **file folder** are created for the group.
- If the tenant switched on *notify administrators about new groups*,
  every system administrator is notified — **once per group**. There is no
  switch on this endpoint to suppress that; it is a tenant setting, and it
  is off unless somebody turned it on. Check it before importing a few
  hundred groups.
- Each creation invalidates the tenant's cache. Nothing breaks, but do not
  fire hundreds of creates back to back — see the pacing note in the sync
  guide.

Group **updates stay out of API v1**. This endpoint creates; renaming,
changing the type or visibility, and membership all remain in Kibi
itself. Calling it twice therefore creates two groups — it is not an
upsert. Ask `GET /api/v1/groups?external_id=…` first if your sync may run
against groups it already wrote.

A **409** means the external id is already mapped to something in this
tenant — possibly a wiki page, a task or a group you cannot see, since
`integration + external_id` is unique across every entity type. No group
is created in that case; pick a different id.

release note in a Git repository) and writes through to it. The
integration namespace comes from the API token, not from the payload —
a token without an integration slug is rejected with 422.

mapped post was updated. This is the endpoint a one-way sync should use:
it removes both the "does it exist yet?" lookup before every write and
the need to keep a mapping table on the integrator's side.

A post that was **deleted** in Kibi keeps its mapping, so writing to its
external id again restores that post and updates it — answer **200**, not
201: the post still carries its history and comments. Permission to
update the post is enough to bring it back.

`external_id` travels in the **body**, not in the path, so it can be
whatever your source system calls the object: a file path
(`releases/2026/08.md`), an opaque SharePoint item id
(`01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP`), a numeric key (`12345t62124`). Slashes, spaces
and umlauts need no URL encoding. Choose an id that survives a rename or
a move — a path does not, and a moved file then arrives as a second post
instead of an update to this one.

The `body` field accepts plain text or TipTap JSON (see
"Rich Text Content Format"), or an HTML/Markdown string when
`content_format` says so; omitting it leaves the existing body
untouched on update. `group_id` is honoured **on creation only** — a post
can carry several groups, and this endpoint will not rewrite that set.

per post. Set `notify` to `false` to write the post quietly; that is what
a first import or a re-sync wants, where a few hundred posts arriving at
once should not land in everybody's inbox. It defaults to `true`, so
leaving it out keeps the behaviour you have today.

The flag covers creating **and** updating, including the update that
follows a restore. That second case matters more than it looks: a post
Kibi has never announced is announced on its next update, so without the
flag a re-sync of old posts would announce all of them at once.

in the body are notified either way — that message is addressed to a
person, not to the workforce. Webhook subscribers still receive
`post.created` / `post.updated`.

not see (`external_id` is unique across the whole tenant). Visibility
wins over uniqueness: the post is neither revealed nor edited, and the
sync has to pick a different id.

read to keep the sync from overwriting an edit somebody made meanwhile —
the write is then refused with **412** instead. On the create path the
header is satisfied by definition: there is no earlier state. Every
response carries a fresh `Last-Modified` for your next write.

### Read back by your own id

This is how you find a page again that your integration wrote through
`PUT /api/v1/wiki/by-external-id` — the counterpart to the write
path, and the reason you never have to keep a table of Kibi ULIDs:

```bash
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer kbc_..." \
  "https://<tenant>.kibi.de/api/v1/wiki?external_id=01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP"
```

**The answer is a collection, not a single page.** `integration +
external_id` is unique across the tenant, so `data` holds either exactly
one entry or none — read `data[0]` and treat the empty array as "nothing
     * is mapped to this id yet". A missing mapping is **not** a 404 here; the
only error case is 422 for a token without an integration slug.

The id sits in the query string, so unlike the upsert body it has to be
**URL-encoded**: `ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx` goes over the wire as
`ordner%2F%C3%9Cnterlagen%202026.docx`.

The list never shows soft-deleted pages, so it is no existence check:
an external id can be taken by something this endpoint does not return.
Only the upsert answers that question reliably.

Creates a new wiki page. Requires the `wiki.create` permission on the
account the token belongs to (WIKI_CREATOR holds it by default).
The `content` field accepts either a **plain text string** (auto-wrapped in a single paragraph)
or a **TipTap JSON document** (see "Rich Text Content Format" in the API overview for all
available node types including headings, lists, tables, callouts, step lists, and more).
Optionally nest under a parent page via parent_id.

Send `content_format` as `html` or `markdown` to write `content` as a
string in that format instead; it is converted to a TipTap document
before it is stored. Without the field nothing changes.

### Syncing? Use the external id instead

This endpoint always creates a new page and answers with a fresh ULID
that you would have to store on your side. If the page originates from
a system of yours — a file in SharePoint, Markdown in a Git repository —
address it by **your own id** instead and let Kibi keep the mapping:

```bash
# Creates on the first call (201), updates the very same page on every
# call after that (200). No ULID bookkeeping on your side.
curl -X PUT "https://<tenant>.kibi.de/api/v1/wiki/by-external-id" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer kbc_..." \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{
        "external_id": "01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP",
        "title": "Onboarding",
        "content": "# Welcome\n\nFirst day checklist.",
        "content_format": "markdown",
        "notify": false
      }'
```

The response carries the mapping back:

```json
{
  "data": {
    "id": "01j8x...",
    "title": "Onboarding",
    "external_ref": {
      "integration": "sharepoint",
      "external_id": "01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP",
      "content_hash": "e3b0c442...",
      "last_synced_at": "2026-09-02T07:12:00+00:00"
    }
  }
}
```

### Which id to pick

`external_id` is **your** id, and Kibi never interprets it: a SharePoint
item id (`01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP`), a Jira key (`PROJ-4711`), a numeric
primary key (`12345t62124`) and a file path (`docs/onboarding.md`) are
all equally valid. It travels in the request body, so slashes, spaces and
umlauts need no URL encoding — `ordner/Ünterlagen 2026.docx` goes over
the wire as it is.

The one rule: pick something that stays the same when the object is
**renamed or moved**. A path is the obvious candidate and the wrong one —
move the file one folder up and the next sync no longer recognises the
page it wrote last week, so it creates a second one and the first goes
stale. Every system that has an opaque id (SharePoint, Jira, most
databases) is better addressed by that id, with the path carried in the
title or the content.

The `integration` comes from your API token, never from the payload.
Find the page again with `GET /api/v1/wiki?external_id=01ABCDEF2GHIJK3LMNOP`.
The full walkthrough is in *Syncing an external system with Kibi* in the
overview.

type.description: **For display only.** The group's type as a person sees it in Kibi, translated into the tenant's language — `"Projekt"`, `"Abteilung"`. The wording changes with the tenant's language, so never compare against it and never send it back. Read `type_slug` for that.

host_email.description:
Who holds the meeting — not who owns the token. A booking system
creates appointments for several people, and the link belongs in
the meeting list of the person who was booked.

The appointment's id in the calling system. Without it the link
is only addressable by the Kibi id returned here.

StoreDmsDocumentRequest.description:
POST /api/v1/dms/documents — single-shot multipart document upload.

`folder_ulid` is deliberately NOT validated with an exists rule: the
controller resolves it through the 404-no-leak path (unknown ulids and
folders outside the DMS subtree answer alike). Authorization is a
pass-through — the controller authorizes against the folder create
policy (DmsFolderAcl) after resolving the target.

Larger files than the single-shot ceiling must use the chunked flow of
the Files V2 API (POST /api/v2/files/uploads) — mirrored limit contract.
StoreDmsDocumentRequest.title: StoreDmsDocumentRequest

type_slug.description:
The group type as a **slug**, not a label — `GET /api/v1/groups/types`
lists every slug this tenant accepts under `value`, standard and
tenant-specific. Defaults to `miscellaneous`. `department` and
`location` are HR-managed and rejected with 422 unless the token's
account may manage them. This is the same field the response returns
as `type_slug`.

type.description:
**Deprecated — send `type_slug`.** An accepted alias for `type_slug`,
and it takes the same slug. It is kept because it was the field name
this endpoint first shipped with; do not build on it. Note that
`type` in the *response* is something else — the translated label —
so echoing that value back here is a 422. When both fields are sent,
`type_slug` wins.

visibility.description:
`all` (default) means everyone who may see groups finds this one;
`members` hides it from everyone but its members. Introducing
`members` needs a token whose account may manage groups — otherwise
the answer is 422.

external_id.description:
Your own stable id for this group in the source system — an ERP project
number (`P-2026-0815`), a cost centre, an opaque directory id. Optional:
without it the group is created unmapped. It travels in the body, so
slashes, spaces and umlauts need no URL encoding. Requires a token with
an integration slug, and answers 409 when the id is already taken.

name.description:
The event title. Required on **every** call, updates included — unlike wiki
pages, tasks and posts, an event is defined by when it happens, so `name`,
`day` and a time travel with each request. A sync mirroring the other side
sends them anyway.

Plain text, exactly as on `POST` and `PUT /api/v1/calendar/events`. Calendar

response returns the HTML rendered from it. That HTML is what `content_hash`
is computed over.

rrule.description:
An RRULE string (`FREQ=WEEKLY;BYDAY=MO,WE`) describing the recurrence, or omit for
a one-off event. Sending an explicit `null` clears an existing series on update.

notify.description:

group_id.description:

groups, and honouring this on update would detach the others and quietly
change who sees the post.

meant for a first import of many posts. Defaults to true, so existing
callers keep the behaviour they have. Never silences @mention
notifications or webhooks.

StoreWebhookEndpointRequest.description:
Dieselben Regeln wie die v2-Verwaltung, plus die external_id.

Die ist hier Pflicht und nicht optional: ohne Mapping gehoert der Endpunkt
niemandem, und die API koennte ihn danach weder finden noch loeschen.

items.description:
Rule::enum und nicht Rule::in: die Fehlermeldung nennt dann den
erlaubten Wertebereich, statt nur "ist ungueltig" zu sagen.

StoreWebhookEndpointRequest.title: StoreWebhookEndpointRequest

UpdateWebhookEndpointRequest.description:
Wie StoreWebhookEndpointRequest, aber ohne external_id: das Mapping wird
beim Anlegen vergeben und ist danach die Identitaet des Endpunkts. Es
nachtraeglich umzuhaengen waere ein Eigentuemerwechsel per PUT.

Achtung fuer kuenftige Regeln: FormRequest-Validierung laeuft VOR
`WebhookEndpointController::ownedEndpoint()`. Die 404-statt-403-Zusage fuer
einen fremden oder UI-angelegten Endpunkt gilt nur, solange keine Regel
hier ressourcenbewusst ist — eine `Rule::unique()` etwa, die gegen DIESEN
Endpunkt prueft, wuerde ueber ihren Fehlertext zu einer Existenz-Oracle:
ein Aufrufer koennte am Validierungsverhalten ablesen, ob eine ULID
ueberhaupt existiert, bevor das Eigentum je geprueft wurde.

Whether deliveries should be sent. Optional: leave it out and the
endpoint keeps whatever state it already had — omitting this field
does NOT mean "turn it off". Send `true` explicitly to bring an
endpoint Kibi auto-disabled after repeated failures back into
service; that is also the only way this request resets the
failure counter and the disabled timestamp.

id.description: The endpoint's ULID. Use it in the path of the update and delete endpoints.

name.description: The human-readable label shown in Kibi's administration.

url.description: Where Kibi POSTs the signed event.

events.description: The events this endpoint is subscribed to. See `GET /api/v1/webhook-endpoints/events` for the full list.

is_active.description: Whether deliveries are currently being sent. Kibi sets this to false on its own after repeated delivery failures.

consecutive_failures.description: How many deliveries failed in a row. Reset to 0 by the next success. A rising number here is the first sign your receiver is down.

last_delivered_at.description: When a delivery last succeeded (ISO 8601), or null if none ever has.

disabled_at.description: When Kibi switched the endpoint off after repeated failures (ISO 8601), or null.

Endpoints created through `POST /api/v1/webhook-endpoints` always carry one, because the mapping is what makes them yours.
